paper.code_data_availability: Replication package listed in the references: Fluchtmann, Jonas, Anita M. …

registers.name_in_paper: Joblog (job application registrations, delivered by STAR)
registers.role: treatment / main explanatory variable: the applied-for jobs

registers.name_in_paper: DREAM, Event History in Public Transfer Programs
registers.role: sample frame: administrative data on UI payments used to define UI spells
sample frame and controls: benefit payments and labor market information
outcomes: monthly earnings, hours, occupation and firm identifiers for the new job; input to the AKM wage regression and the typical-wage prediction

registers.name_in_paper: IDA, Integrated Database for Labor Market Research
registers.role: linkage and controls: worker and firm characteristics, employment history, industry and occupation

registers.name_in_paper: Auxiliary survey data on Danish UI recipients (online Appendix A.9.1)
Audit study data from Ahmed, Granberg, and Khanna (2021), covering three Swedish audit studies conducted between 2016 and 2019
registers.role: external comparison: occupation-level gender gaps in callback rates

linkages: UI recipients linked to their Joblog job applications via a unique person identifier
UI recipients linked to demographic information, education, and the full history of public benefit payments and employment via the person identifier (DREAM, ILME, BFL, IDA)
each job application linked to a firm and an occupation by string matching on job title, firm name and firm address (86 percent of applications matched to a firm, 82 percent to an occupation)
firms linked to AKM firm fixed effects estimated on the universe of Danish workers and firms
applied-for jobs and new jobs linked to a predicted (“typical”) wage from a model estimated on observed wages in new jobs
jobs linked to implied commuting times computed from the individual's municipality of residence and the job's postal code using the Google Maps API
firms linked to a family-friendliness measure based on average parental leave taken when an employee or their partner gives birth
residual hiring gaps by occupation matched to occupation-level callback gaps from Ahmed, Granberg, and Khanna (2021)

sample.universe: all UI recipients of Danish nationality entering new UI spells from September 2015 to September 2017
sample.unit_of_observation: UI spell (individual-spell); job applications are aggregated into shares within the spell; job types (occupations, industries, wage-level deciles) are the unit for the correlation and segregation measures
selection_rules: base sample: all UI recipients of Danish nationality entering new UI spells from September 2015 to September 2017 (DREAM, ILME)
1. only UI spells lasting at least eight weeks
2. only individuals who registered at least four job applications during their spell
3. only UI spells that end with the individual finding a job within one year
4. job applications made in the last four weeks before a transition to employment are excluded
applications with missing information on the relevant job characteristic are excluded
descriptive analysis: individuals with an estimated propensity score above 0.99 or below 0.01 are excluded, reducing the sample of UI spells by 5.4 percent
decomposition: a second trimming on the propensity score including application behavior, making the decomposition sample 7.1 percent smaller than the descriptive sample
sample.n_observations: 114,375 UI spells with 2,911,585 job applications (before propensity-score trimming)

construction_notes: Wages in Figure 1 are winsorised at the fifth and ninety-fifth percentile.
The hourly wage is constructed from monthly earnings in the administrative registers and measured one month after entering a new job.

Firm wage level is the firm fixed effect from an Abowd-Kramarz-Margolis log wage regression with worker and firm fixed effects estimated on the universe of Danish workers and firms; the main measure standardizes these effects within industry, and non-standardized effects are also reported.

The “typical wage” of a job is a predicted wage from a model of observed wages in new jobs on the full set of job characteristics, computed for both applied-for jobs and actual new jobs; online Appendix B.6 computes typical wages separately by gender.
Occupation and industry of applied-for jobs are assigned by string matching on job title, firm name and firm address; 86 percent of applications are matched to a firm and 82 percent to an occupation.

Observables are conditioned out by propensity-score reweighting: women are weighted by p-hat/(1 - p-hat) from a logit propensity score for being male, using 332 variables selected by double-LASSO (Belloni, Chernozhukov, and Hansen 2014) from a baseline set of 4,196 variables covering age, work experience, level and field of education, prior industries and occupations and dependence on public transfers, all interacted with age, years of education, total work experience and experience over the last five years.

Standard errors for Tables 2, 3 and 4 come from 2,000 bootstrap samples that resample unemployment spells and reestimate the propensity scores and the gaps/decomposition; confidence bars in Figures 2 and 5 use standard errors clustered on the individual level.
Commuting times are computed with the Google Maps API from the individual's municipality of residence and the job's postal code.

Family friendliness of a firm is the average parental leave taken when an employee or their partner gives birth, corrected for the gender of the employee, with firms that never experience a birth kept as a separate category.

Survey-based validity checks estimate that the Joblog data cover between 69 and 80 percent of all applied-for jobs (68-82 percent for women, 72-76 percent for men), and 47 percent of new hires can be linked to a registered application against a benchmark of 43-50 percent.

claims.statement: Among observationally similar men and women, the occupational segregation measured over job applications is 0.187.

treatment.label: Gender (men versus women) as the grouping variable of the segregation index

definition.value: The Duncan index is computed over the application (or hiring) shares of the average woman and the average man, after propensity-score reweighting the women to have the same labor market observables as the men; it has no signed direction.

timing.value: Fixed individual characteristic.

outcome.label: Duncan index of occupational segregation across 1-digit occupations, computed on application shares

register_source.value: Joblog job application records (STAR 2019); occupation and industry of the applied-for job assigned by string matching on job title, firm name and firm address and merged to Statistics Denmark firm data (BFL, IDA)

definition.value: Duncan index of gender segregation (Duncan and Duncan 1955), computed on the propensity-score reweighted sample as (1/2)*sum_y |a^w_y - a^m_y| over the nine 1-digit occupations, where a^w_y and a^m_y are the shares of applications sent to job type y by the average woman and the average man. Applied to applications it measures the fraction of the average woman's (or man's) applications that would have to be changed to eliminate the gender application gap.

timing.value: Applications registered in Joblog during the UI spell, excluding those made in the last four weeks before the transition to employment

units.value: index units (fraction of applications that would have to be reallocated)

estimand.target_population: UI recipients of Danish nationality entering new UI spells between September 2015 and September 2017 who find a job within one year, with women reweighted to men's observables

population.description: UI recipients of Danish nationality entering new UI spells from September 2015 to September 2017, after four sample restrictions and propensity-score trimming
population.selection: UI spells of at least eight weeks, with at least four registered applications, ending in a hire within one year; propensity score between 0.01 and 0.99

identification.source_of_variation: none: a gender comparison within a propensity-score reweighted sample of UI recipients, with no exogenous variation claimed

key_assumptions.assumption: Propensity-score reweighting on the LASSO-selected labor market observables x makes the distribution of observables among women the same as among men, so the residual difference compares observationally similar men and women; the logit propensity-score model is correctly specified.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 reports means for men, women raw and women reweighted; footnote 20 notes that reweighting need not impose exact balance in finite samples and reports an exact-balance robustness check (online Appendix B.3).

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support / overlap of the propensity score: individuals with an estimated propensity score above 0.99 or below 0.01 are excluded.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The trimming is reported to reduce the sample of UI spells by 5.4 percent (online Appendix Table A.1).

key_assumptions.assumption: The Joblog data capture applied-for jobs with high coverage and the registered subset is representative of all applied-for jobs, similarly so for men and women.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Survey-based coverage estimates of 69-80 percent, similar by gender; predictive-power and hire-matching validity checks (Section IIC, online Appendix A.9).

key_assumptions.assumption: The analysis sample is conditioned on UI spells that end with the individual finding a job within one year (and on at least eight weeks of UI and at least four registered applications).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Sample restrictions listed in Section IIA; online Appendix B.1 varies them.
